If you already have a breathing problem like asthma or emphysema, stress can make it even harder to breathe. Under stress, your heart also pumps faster. Stress hormones cause your blood vessels to constrict and divert more oxygen to your muscles so you’ll have more strength to take action. But this also raises your blood pressure. passages.text: Stress triggers the body’s fight-or-flight response. Chronic stress can cause negative health effects on your mood, immune and digestive systems, and cardiovascular health. You’re sitting in traffic, late for an important meeting, watching the minutes tick away. Your hypothalamus, a tiny control tower in your brain, decides to send out the order: Send in the stress hormones! These stress hormones are the same ones that trigger your body’s “fight or flight” response. Your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles ready for action. This response was designed to protect your body in an emergency by preparing you to react quickly. But when the stress response keeps firing, day after day, it could put your health at serious risk. A healthy way to deal with stress is to focus on what you can control. For example, you might ask for help, do fewer tasks or let go of trying to be perfect when you can. Taking small steps such as these can help you feel less overwhelmed. Your thoughts also affect how you feel and act. If you always think the worst is going to happen, your stress grows. When the natural stress response becomes overactive The body's stress response system usually helps you handle tough situations. It turns itself on and off as needed. Once a perceived threat has passed, hormones return to typical levels. As adrenaline and cortisol levels drop, your heart rate and blood pressure return to typical levels. Other systems go back to their regular activities. But when stressors are always present and you always feel stressed, that fight-or-flight reaction stays turned on. This may happen when you are dealing with chronic stress or worrying about the future. When the stress response system is active for too long, it can give you too much exposure to cortisol and other stress hormones. That can disrupt almost all the body's processes. How you react to your life stressors is affected by your genetics and your life experiences. The demands of life also play a role. - Genes. Your genes help shape how you react to stress. This is why some people are naturally laid-back, while others tend to respond quickly to even the slightest stressor. - Life experiences. Examples of trauma include experiencing abuse or neglect as a child or being in a car accident. When you face a perceived threat, a tiny area at the brain's base, called the hypothalamus, sets off an alarm system in the body. An example of a perceived threat is a large dog barking at you during your morning walk. Through nerve and hormonal signals, this alarm system prompts the adrenal glands, found atop the kidneys, to release a surge of hormones, such as adrenaline and cortisol. Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster, causes blood pressure to go up and gives you more energy. Cortisol, the main stress hormone, increases sugar, also called glucose, in the blood. It also helps the brain use glucose more effectively. It also increases the availability of substances in the body that repair tissues. Cortisol also slows body functions that are not needed or harmful in a fight-or-flight situation. It changes immune system responses and makes it harder for the digestive system, the reproductive system and growth processes to work. When to ask for help If you’ve taken steps to manage your stress but you keep having symptoms, see your healthcare professional. Your healthcare professional may want to check for other potential causes. You also could see a counselor or therapist. This person can help you find sources of stress and learn new coping skills.
